notes: hellfire-club reflects her Krakoa-era role as Red Queen of the Hellfire Trading Company. 'Star-Lord' is omitted as an alias because it belongs to Peter Quill.

name: Klaw
caseNote: Subject is a sound-based villain whose vibranium converter replaced the hand he lost to the Black Panther. Has served with the Frightful Four. Subject is insured against noise.
notes: Live action Klaue (Andy Serkis) first in Age of Ultron.

name: Knull
caseNote: Subject is a primordial god of darkness who created the symbiotes and the living blade All-Black. Once sealed Earth inside a sphere of symbiote dragons. Agents are advised to carry a flashlight.
notes: The infobox lists an unnamed figure in Thor: God of Thunder #6 (March 2013), later identified as Knull, before his full debut in Venom vol. 4 #3 (August 2018), so the debut year is contested. Origin set to deity (a primordial god); Venom: The Last Dance is a Sony film, not MCU.

name: Korath the Pursuer
caseNote: Subject is a Kree warrior and long-time soldier of Ronan. Pursues targets until they are caught or he is not. Agents are advised not to be caught.
notes: mcu: Djimon Hounsou played Korath in GotG (2014) per film cast; no snippet in mcu_matches. Not confirmed in this session.

name: Kraglin
caseNote: Subject is an A-Chilitarian who served as Yondu's second-in-command. Joined the Guardians after the Ravagers broke up. Agents are advised not to ask about the arrow.
notes: Alignment: MCU Kraglin moves from Ravagers to Guardians; hero arguable.

name: Kraven the Hunter
caseNote: Subject is Sergei Kravinoff, a big-game hunter who regards Spider-Man as the most dangerous game. Maintains superhuman strength and slowed aging with a potion of jungle herbs. Agents should not wear animal print in his presence.
notes: Origin is contested: his potion is described both as a 'mystical serum' and as jungle herbs, and Wikipedia classes him as human mutate. A silhouette of Kraven in the No Way Home sky is not counted as a live-action appearance, and the 2024 film is Sony's.

name: Kro
caseNote: Subject is a Deviant warlord and long-time enemy of the Eternals. Appeared in the film Eternals only as a voice-acted CGI character. Subject has no known hobbies other than war.
notes: MCU appearance is voice-only (Bill Skarsgard), which does not count. Deviants are not in the teams vocabulary.

name: Kurse
caseNote: Subject was the Dark Elf Algrim the Strong until the Beyonder rebuilt him as the armored Kurse. Pursued Thor obsessively over a betrayal that was Malekith's doing. Agents should confirm the target before filing a grudge.
notes: Debuted as Algrim in Thor #347 (Sep 1984) and first appeared as Kurse in Secret Wars II #4 (Oct 1985); the Beyonder's empowerment makes cosmic arguable. He later repented and was granted Asgardian citizenship, and a second Kurse (Waziria) exists.

name: Lady Bullseye
caseNote: Subject is a lawyer turned assassin inspired by Bullseye. Trained in martial arts and a skilled marksman. Agents are advised that her briefcase is not for filing.
notes: Wikipedia gives few affiliations; Hand membership noted as informal.

name: Lady Deathstrike
caseNote: Subject is a cyborg with adamantium-laced claws and a grudge against Wolverine. Her father was the original adamantium bonding engineer. Agents are advised not to be underweight.
notes: Debut: Yuriko Oyama in Daredevil #197 (Aug 1983) used per infobox; first as Lady Deathstrike is Alpha Flight #33 (Apr 1986).

name: Laufey
caseNote: Subject is king of the Frost Giants and the biological father of Loki. Usually depicted as an enemy of Odin. Family reunions are not recommended.
notes: No standalone article or infobox; debut taken from Wikipedia's List of Marvel Comics characters: L.

name: Lilandra
caseNote: Subject is a Shi'ar empress who deposed her mad sibling and allied with the X-Men. Rules a galactic empire. Agents are advised that she is also bigger than the entire agency.

name: Lilith
caseNote: Subject is the vampire daughter of Dracula who has opposed her father. Has worked with S.H.I.E.L.D.'s Paranormal Containment Unit. Agents are advised not to mention family.
notes: Infobox lists Giant-Size Chillers Featuring the Curse of Dracula #1 (1974-06).

name: Living Brain
caseNote: Subject is a robot billed as the most intelligent computer in existence. Has since been reprogrammed as a lab assistant at Parker Industries. Agents are advised to locate the off switch before engaging.
notes: It was briefly part of Boomerang's Marvel NOW! Sinister Six before The Superior Foes of Spider-Man dropped it, so that is treated as a one-off. Wikipedia refers to the robot as 'it'.

name: Living Laser
caseNote: Subject is a physicist who converted himself into living laser light. Has fought the Avengers and Iron Man. Agents are advised to avoid mirrors.
notes: Origin could also be tech (self-built device).

name: Living Tribunal
caseNote: Subject is a three-faced cosmic judge charged with keeping balance across the multiverse. Once moved to destroy Earth until Doctor Strange argued the planet's case. Agents are advised not to appeal Subject's rulings.
notes: MCU set to false. Wikipedia calls its Multiverse of Madness moment a cameo, but only statues or heads of the Tribunal are shown there and in Loki. A neutral judge written mostly as 'it', so alignment and gender are contested.

name: Lizard
caseNote: Subject is Dr. Curt Connors, a former army surgeon who lost his right arm and developed a lizard-DNA serum to regrow it. The serum worked, with side effects. Connors and the Lizard do not share priorities.
notes: The infobox lists the Sinister Six, but his comics membership was a one-off during Civil War, so it is not counted.

name: Lockjaw
caseNote: Subject is a giant bulldog who teleports himself and others across any distance. Serves as transport for the Inhuman Royal Family. Good boy.

name: Loki
caseNote: Subject is a Frost Giant by birth, adopted by Odin and raised as Thor's brother. His schemes inadvertently led to the formation of the Avengers. Statements by Subject are not to be entered into the record without corroboration.
notes: Infobox lists a Golden Age Loki in Venus #6 (Aug 1949) ahead of the modern Loki's Journey into Mystery #85 (Oct 1962); the rubric takes the earliest, though most players will expect 1962. Usually a villain with antihero runs, and written as genderfluid at times (Lady Loki, Agent of Asgard, the MCU) though primarily male.

name: Longshot
caseNote: Subject is an artificial lifeform from the Mojoverse whose powers bend probability in his favor, provided his intentions are good. Escaped the television tyrant Mojo and joined the X-Men. Agents are advised not to bet against him.
notes: Wikipedia gives his species as 'Artificial Mojoverse lifeform' and his alter ego as 'No dual identity'. Origin is set to alien (an engineered extradimensional being), though synthetic is arguable and he is not a mutant.

name: Lorelei
caseNote: Subject is an Asgardian and the younger sister of Amora the Enchantress. Has used enchanted golden mead as a love potion. Personnel are advised to bring their own drinks.
notes: Her live-action role in Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. does not count toward mcu.

name: Luke Cage
caseNote: Subject gained unbreakable skin and super strength from a prison experiment. Founded Heroes for Hire and later joined the Avengers. Agents are advised that bullets are a poor opening argument.
notes: Mike Colter appears in Born Again only in the season 2 finale. Netflix's Luke Cage does not count.

name: Lyja
caseNote: Subject is a Skrull spy who first impersonated Alicia Masters. Later married Johnny Storm before returning to her people. Agents are advised to verify identities at all weddings.
notes: Debut is as Alicia Masters (Fantastic Four #265); first appearance as Lyja is #357 (1991-10). Alignment contested: antihero vs villain.

name: M.O.D.O.K.
aliases: Mental Organism Designed Only for Killing
caseNote: Subject underwent A.I.M. mutagenic experiments that vastly enlarged both his intellect and his head. Travels by hoverchair and wields psionic powers. Hat size remains classified.
notes: Wikipedia's infobox gives Tales of Suspense #94 (October 1967), but its lead and publication history name #93 (September 1967) as the first appearance, so #93 is used. The MCU's M.O.D.O.K. is Darren Cross (Corey Stoll), not George Tarleton.

name: M'Baku
caseNote: Subject is the Jabari warrior known as Man-Ape and a long-standing rival of Black Panther. Has been villain and later ally. Agents are advised to avoid mountains.
notes: Resolved page was wrong; Man-Ape debut and details used. Alignment contested: villain in comics, MCU ally.

name: Machine Man
caseNote: Subject is an android built for the military that developed free will. Has served with S.H.I.E.L.D. and the Avengers. Agents are advised to treat it politely.
notes: Primary team unclear.

name: Mad Thinker
caseNote: Subject is a criminal genius who plans to the last detail and builds android pawns. Repeat opponent of the Fantastic Four. Agents may bet against him on any given day.
notes: No known real name; realName left empty.

name: Madame Masque
caseNote: Subject is a crime figure who wears a golden mask to hide scars. Has been both an enemy and lover of Iron Man. Agents are advised not to ask about the mask.
notes: Alignment contested.

name: Madame Web
caseNote: Subject is Cassandra Webb, a blind clairvoyant and precognitive mutant who long depended on a web-shaped life-support system. Has used her abilities to help Spider-Man on several occasions. Meetings with Subject need not be scheduled; she will already know.
notes: This entry is Cassandra Webb, the original; Julia Carpenter later inherited the name. The 2024 Sony film is not MCU and gives her a spider-bite origin, unlike the comics' mutant.

name: Maggott
caseNote: Subject is a South African mutant with slugs in his abdomen that digest matter. Was a member of Generation X and the X-Men. Agents are advised not to ask about lunch.
notes: Infobox gives 1997 only; April 1997 cover date assumed from the issue. Verify month.

name: Magik
caseNote: Subject teleports via stepping discs through the demon dimension Limbo, which she rules as its sorceress. Younger sister of Colossus; aged seven years in Limbo while no time passed on Earth. Agents are advised not to follow her through glowing circles.
notes: The 1975 debut is Illyana as a child; the infobox also lists her debut as Magik in Magik #1 (Dec 1983). She is a mutant whose sorcery was acquired in Limbo, and Wikipedia calls her a superhero, though her Darkchilde side could support antihero.

name: Magma
caseNote: Subject is a Roman-descended mutant from the lost Nova Roma who controls lava and heat. Has served the New Mutants and the X-Men. Agents are advised against asking about the volcano.
notes: Alignment has swung between hero and villain (Hellfire Club, Hellions) but is most commonly hero.

name: Magneto
caseNote: Subject controls magnetic fields and holds strong views on mutant survival. Has led the Brotherhood, served as an X-Man and sat on Krakoa's Quiet Council. Agents are advised to remove metal fillings before interview.
notes: Villain by origin, antihero by long tenure as protector of mutants; rubric treats side-switching as antihero.

name: Magus
caseNote: Subject is the dark aspect of Adam Warlock and has ruled the Universal Church of Truth. Has repeatedly tried to claim the Infinity Gems. Agents are advised that Subject is, quite literally, his own worst enemy.
notes: The name is ambiguous: Wikipedia's 'Magus (Marvel Comics)' is the Technarch father of Warlock (New Mutants #18, 1984). Given this cosmic batch, this record is Adam Warlock's evil self, covered in the Adam Warlock article without an infobox; the debut is from its Strange Tales #178 citation.

name: Major Victory
caseNote: Subject is a 20th-century astronaut who aged in a centuries-long journey. Founding member of the 31st-century Guardians. Agents are reminded that he is not Marvel Boy.

name: Makkari
caseNote: Subject is the Eternal speedster, associated with Mercury and Hermes. Has used the aliases Mercury and Hurricane. Agents attempting pursuit are advised to arrive early.
notes: Gender contested: male in comics, female in the MCU (Lauren Ridloff). Earlier alias debuts in 1940 and 1941 exist.

name: Malekith
caseNote: Subject rules the Dark Elves of Svartalfheim and has often wielded the Casket of Ancient Winters. Served as the main antagonist of the War of the Realms. Agents should not accept faerie food from Subject.
notes: Dark Elves are treated as a Norse mythological race (deity).

name: Man-Thing
caseNote: Subject is a biochemist transformed into a swamp creature by an experimental serum. Burns those who feel fear. Agents are advised to remain calm.

name: Man-Wolf
caseNote: Subject is astronaut John Jameson, son of J. Jonah Jameson. A gem he found on the Moon turns him into a wolf-like creature. Agents are advised not to schedule meetings during a full moon.
notes: The infobox debut is John Jameson's first appearance; he first became Man-Wolf in ASM #124 (September 1973). Alignment and origin are judgment calls: Jameson is a supporting hero (astronaut, Stargod, Agents of Wakanda), while his Man-Wolf form is a monster powered by the mystical Godstone.

name: Mandarin
caseNote: Subject is a master martial artist whose ten rings, salvaged from a crashed alien starship, each grant a different power. A longtime nemesis of Iron Man. Agents are advised to count the rings before engaging.
notes: mcuFirst is contested: Iron Man 3 has the Mandarin persona (Trevor Slattery as figurehead, Aldrich Killian claiming the title), while Shang-Chi's Xu Wenwu is the closer adaptation but never uses the name himself. The comics never reveal his birth name, so realName is empty.

name: Mangog
caseNote: Subject embodies the hatred of a billion billion beings whose race was defeated by Odin. Has repeatedly sought the Odinsword to end the universe. Subject claims he will exist as long as there is hatred; the bureau has no rebuttal.
notes: Origin is a judgment call: a spell-made living prison embodying an alien race's hatred; magic chosen, alien arguable.

name: Mantis
caseNote: Subject is a martial artist raised by the Priests of Pama and later named the Celestial Madonna. Served with the Avengers and the Guardians. Agents are reminded that she is not an actual insect.
notes: Origin: infobox human mutate; trained or cosmic arguable. primaryTeam: avengers (original tenure) vs guardians (MCU association).

name: Maria Hill
caseNote: Subject is a career intelligence officer who succeeded Nick Fury as director of S.H.I.E.L.D. Has no superhuman abilities and has repeatedly clashed with the Avengers over oversight. Agents should expect an audit.
notes: Infobox lists March 2005 (on-sale date); the April 2005 cover date is used per rubric.

name: Marrow
caseNote: Subject is a mutant with a bone-growing ability and a radical past with the Gene Nation. Later joined the X-Men and Weapon X. Agents are advised to avoid hugging.
notes: Debut as Sarah in Cable #15; as Marrow in X-Men Prime (July 1995). Used first appearance as Sarah.

name: Martinex
caseNote: Subject is the last surviving Pluvian, with crystalline skin engineered for Pluto's harsh conditions. Founding member of the original Guardians of the Galaxy and its resident scientist. Do not mistake Subject for a chandelier.
notes: Pluvians are genetically engineered descendants of human colonists, classed as alien. Ravagers is MCU-only; his Avengers status was honorary during the Korvac Saga and is left out.

name: Marvel Boy (Noh-Varr)
caseNote: Subject is a Kree soldier from an alternate universe, enhanced with insect DNA, who once declared war on Earth. He has since served with the Avengers and the Young Avengers. The declaration remains on file.
notes: He began as a hostile alien who declared war on Earth and served briefly on Osborn's Dark Avengers before turning heroic; inhumans reflects his time with the Royals. Primary team is the Young Avengers (as Marvel Boy), though as Protector he was also a main-roster Avenger; 'Captain Marvel' is left out of aliases.

name: Mastermind (Jason Wyngarde)
caseNote: Subject creates convincing illusions and has used them to manipulate mutants. Corrupted Jean Grey as the Black Queen. Agents are advised not to trust their eyes.

name: Maximus
caseNote: Subject is the brother of Black Bolt and a recurring claimant to the Inhuman throne, with mind-altering abilities. Has been affiliated with the Cabal. Not named as an heir.
notes: The Thor: Love and Thunder match is unrelated (Gladiator film).

name: Medusa
caseNote: Subject is queen of the Inhumans and wife of Black Bolt, with prehensile red hair. Has served with the Fantastic Four and Frightful Four. Agents are advised against brushing.
notes: Appeared as villain in early Frightful Four stories; hero in main history.

name: Meggan
caseNote: Subject is a shapeshifter who mirrors the emotions of those around her. Member of Excalibur and spouse of Brian Braddock. Agents are advised to keep their moods in check.
notes: Origin contested: mutant (empathic shapeshifter) vs magic or other.

name: Mephisto
caseNote: Subject is a demon lord who collects souls and makes deals with the desperate. Has tormented the Silver Surfer, Ghost Rider and others. Agents are advised to read all contracts.
notes: Ironheart is the first live-action title in which the name Mephisto is applied to a character on screen.

name: Mercury
caseNote: Subject is a mutant whose body is a liquid metal resembling mercury, which she can reshape or solidify at will. She trained in the Xavier Institute's Hellions squad. Thermometer jokes are discouraged.
notes: Her teams (Hellions, New X-Men) were Xavier Institute student squads with no TEAMS id, and she never served on an X-Men main roster, so primaryTeam is none.

name: Mirage
debutIssue: Marvel Graphic Novel #4: The New Mutants
caseNote: Subject is a Cheyenne mutant who projects a target's deepest fears or desires as illusions. Has led the New Mutants and served as a Valkyrie. Agents are advised to keep their thoughts tidy.
notes: Page title is Danielle Moonstar.

name: Mister Fantastic
caseNote: Subject is the foremost scientist of his world, whose body stretches after cosmic ray exposure. Founded the Fantastic Four and sits on the Illuminati. Agents are advised not to ask him to hold a door.

name: Mister Hyde
caseNote: Subject is Calvin Zabo, a medical researcher who drew on Jekyll and Hyde to create a formula that turns him into a hulking brute. Has served on several Masters of Evil rosters and the Thunderbolts. Agents are advised his bedside manner has not improved.
notes: Calvin Johnson in Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. does not count for the MCU field because it is an ABC/Marvel Television series.

name: Mister Negative
debutIssue: Free Comic Book Day: The Amazing Spider-Man #1
caseNote: Subject runs a Chinatown soup kitchen as philanthropist Martin Li while leading the Inner Demons gang as Mister Negative. An experimental drug gave him control of the Darkforce and Lightforce. Agents are advised to check both sides of his ledger.
notes: Martin Li is the civilian identity he lives under; Wikipedia says his birth name was never revealed. Spider-Man: Brand New Day only references his gang's logo, so he does not count as appearing.

name: Mister Sinister
caseNote: Subject is a Victorian-era geneticist who has dedicated centuries to engineering mutant bloodlines. Maintains many clones. Agents are advised to keep hair samples private.
notes: Debut: first mentioned #212 (1986), first seen in silhouette #213 (1987-01), full #221 (1987-09). Origin mutate vs mutant arguable.

name: Misty Knight
caseNote: Subject is a former police detective who lost an arm in a bombing. Replaced it with a Stark-built bionic one. Co-leads the Daughters of the Dragon with Colleen Wing.
notes: Origin tech (bionic arm) vs trained is arguable. Her Netflix appearances do not count.

name: Mobius M. Mobius
caseNote: Subject is a Time Variance Authority analyst who keeps the timeline tidy. Prefers jet skis and has a loyalty to his office. Agents are advised that he has paperwork for them.

name: Mockingbird
caseNote: Subject is a biologist and former S.H.I.E.L.D. Agent 19 who fights with battle staves. Founding member of the West Coast Avengers and ex-wife of Hawkeye. Was once declared dead; records were later amended.
notes: Origin contested: a non-powered agent for most of her history, she later gained superhuman abilities from a Super-Soldier Serum/Infinity Formula mix (classed super-soldier). The MCU's 'Agent 19' is Laura Barton, and ABC's Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D. does not count.

name: Moira MacTaggert
caseNote: Subject is a Scottish geneticist who ran the Muir Island research facility and spent decades treating mutants. Her file was later amended to classify her as a mutant herself. Agents should not assume this file is final.
notes: She was a non-powered human scientist for most of her history until House of X (2019) revealed her as a reincarnating mutant, and she later turned against mutants with Orchis before being depowered. Origin (mutant vs trained) and alignment (hero vs villain) are both contested.

name: Mojo
caseNote: Subject is a Spineless One who rules a dimension of television. Broadcasts violence to a captive audience. Agents are advised not to turn on the TV.

name: Mole Man
caseNote: Subject is a rejected surface scientist who rules Subterranea and its monsters. First recorded opponent of the Fantastic Four. Does not enjoy sunlight, gardens, or being described as a mole.

name: Molecule Man
caseNote: Subject is a former lab technician with near-total control over matter after a reactor accident. Shy by temperament and among the most powerful beings on Earth. Agents are advised to be polite.
notes: Alignment mostly villain, though he has acted as an ally in several events.

name: Molly Hayes
caseNote: Subject is the youngest founding member of the Runaways, a mutant with superhuman strength and invulnerability. She is known for her hats. Agents should not mistake her age for weakness.
notes: Allegra Acosta played her in Hulu's Runaways, which does not count toward mcu.

name: Molten Man
caseNote: Subject was coated in an experimental liquid metal alloy during a lab accident, leaving him with metallic skin and heat powers. Is the stepbrother of Liz Allan. Agents are advised not to shake hands.
notes: His only live-action appearance is the Fire Elemental illusion in Spider-Man: Far From Home, which Wikipedia describes as a creature based on Molten Man rather than Mark Raxton himself, so the MCU flag is debatable.

name: Monica Rambeau
caseNote: Subject is a former New Orleans harbor patrol lieutenant who can transform into any form of energy. Led the Avengers in the 1980s as Captain Marvel. Agents should confirm her current codename before filing.
notes: Sources disagree on the annual's month (Wikipedia infobox: October 1982; dealer listings: December 1982), so a year-only date is used. 'Captain Marvel' left out of aliases because the game assigns it to Carol Danvers.

name: Montana
caseNote: Subject is Jackson Brice, a marksman and lariat specialist with the Enforcers. Has spent decades as hired muscle for New York crime bosses. Agents are advised that the cowboy hat is not a disguise.
notes: His MCU appearance is Jackson Brice (Logan Marshall-Green) as the first Shocker in Spider-Man: Homecoming. 'Shocker' is left out of aliases because it belongs to Herman Schultz.

name: Moon Girl
caseNote: Subject is a preteen Inhuman inventor who can swap minds with her partner, Devil Dinosaur. Amadeus Cho has called her the smartest person in the world. Classroom visits should allow for a dinosaur.
notes: Wikipedia has no character infobox: her page redirects to the series article, which gives the November 2015 on-sale launch, while issue #1 is cover-dated January 2016. The animated series makes her human, but in the comics she is an Inhuman.

name: Moon Knight
caseNote: Subject is a former mercenary who serves as the avatar of the Egyptian moon god Khonshu. Operates with several distinct identities. Agents are advised that he does not enjoy being introduced as a bat.
notes: Powers granted by Khonshu make magic defensible; trained chosen because he has no innate powers.

name: Moondragon
caseNote: Subject is the daughter of Drax, a monk-trained telepath on Titan. Has served with the Avengers and Defenders. Agents are advised not to read the minds of Titan's monks.
notes: Origin: trained (Titan monastic discipline, human) vs mutate. Alignment hero with villainous periods; antihero arguable. Infobox gives Madame MacEvil debut Iron Man #54 (Jan 1973) and Moondragon debut Daredevil #105.

name: Moonstone
caseNote: Subject is a psychiatrist who gained powers from an alien gravity stone. Has served with the Masters of Evil, the Thunderbolts and the Dark Avengers. Agents are advised not to accept therapy from her.
notes: Unreliable infobox (list page, Mad Merlin/Journey into Mystery #96) was ignored; Karla Sofen article used. Debut is Karla Sofen (Captain America #192); Moonstone identity first appears Incredible Hulk #228 (1978-10). Alignment villain vs antihero and origin (tech vs cosmic) contested. Other characters have used the Moonstone name.

name: Morbius
caseNote: Subject is Michael Morbius, a Nobel Prize-winning biochemist who tried to cure a rare blood disease with vampire bat DNA and electroshock. He survived as a pseudo-vampire who must drink human blood. Blood drives in his vicinity should be postponed.
notes: Primary team could also be the Legion of Monsters (founding member, 2011 series); the Midnight Sons was chosen for his core role in the 1992 crossover. The 2022 Morbius film is Sony's, not MCU.

name: Morg
caseNote: Subject is a former court executioner who betrayed his own people before Galactus made him a herald. Wields the Power Cosmic and a double-bladed axe. Agents are advised not to request a reference.

name: Morgan le Fay
caseNote: Subject is the half-sister of King Arthur and a powerful sorceress. A longtime foe of the Black Knight and Avengers. Agents are advised not to accept anything she bakes.

name: Morlun
caseNote: Subject is a psychic vampire of extreme age who feeds on the life force of spider-totems. Has hunted Spider-Man and his counterparts across the multiverse with his family, the Inheritors. Agents with spider-powers should request desk duty.

name: Ms. Marvel (Kamala Khan)
caseNote: Subject is a Jersey City teenager and devoted Avengers fan whose powers emerged when the Terrigen Mists spread. Can stretch, shrink and embiggen at will. Co-founded the Champions; her fan fiction remains under review.
notes: Origin contested: Inhuman via Terrigenesis in comics (classed inhuman), but a 2023 retcon added a dormant X-gene and the MCU portrays her as a mutant. Debut uses the background cameo the infobox lists (full debut: All-New Marvel Now! Point One #1, 2014).

name: Multiple Man
caseNote: Subject creates duplicates of himself by taking a physical impact. Serves as a private investigator with X-Factor Investigations. Agents are advised to count heads before dismissal.
notes: Origin mutant (X-gene, per article) vs mutate (powers triggered by childhood radiation exposure). Defenders listing is minor and left out.

name: Muse
caseNote: Subject is a serial killer who stages mass killings into street art. His ghost later guided a second Muse. Agents are advised not to critique the work.
notes: Two Muses: first is Inhuman Vincent van Gore (used), second Morgan Whittier is human (debut 2025). Born Again season 1 depicts Bastian Cooper as the Muse killer; Heather Glenn's Muse is season 3.

name: Mysterio
caseNote: Subject is Quentin Beck, a special-effects artist and stuntman who turned his illusions to crime after his film career stalled. Has no superhuman powers, only smoke, holograms and a fishbowl helmet. Nothing Subject shows you should be believed.
notes: Others have used the Mysterio identity; this entry is Quentin Beck.

name: Mystique
caseNote: Subject is a shapeshifting mutant, spy and long-time Brotherhood leader. Has adopted the face of agents, senators and, once, a lover. Agents should request a password from everyone, including Subject's supervisor.
notes: Infobox debut field is empty; Ms. Marvel #16 (Jan 1978) taken from article lead. Alignment villain vs antihero is arguable; X-Men membership is brief.

name: Nakia
caseNote: Subject was raised as a Dora Milaje and later became the villain Malice after T'Challa rejected her. Hostile to those close to him. Agents should avoid dating the King.
notes: Origin contested: infobox says human mutate, text says magical ritual. MCU Nakia is a spy, adapted from the comics character. Alignment contested (comics villain, MCU hero).

name: Namor
caseNote: Subject is the Atlantean king and mutant who flies and possesses superhuman strength. Marvel's first antihero who has fought both the surface world and its enemies. Agents are advised to be polite.
notes: Debut via Marvel Comics #1 (the uncirculated Motion Picture Funnies Weekly is ignored). Origin as Atlantean-mutant hybrid; could also be argued alien.

name: Namora
caseNote: Subject is Namor's cousin, a super-strong Atlantean heroine. Has served with Agents of Atlas. Family reunions are loud.
notes: Alias Aquaria Nautica Neptunia included as alias only. Origin hybrid mutant; MCU version is Talokan lieutenant.

name: Nebula
caseNote: Subject is a Luphomoid space pirate who claimed to be Thanos's granddaughter. Moved from enemy of the Avengers to a Guardian. Agents are advised to bring a thick-skinned negotiator.
notes: Alignment: villain early, antihero later; the side-switching rule gives antihero.

name: Nick Fury
debutIssue: Sgt. Fury and His Howling Commandos #1
caseNote: Subject is a World War II veteran who led the Howling Commandos before directing S.H.I.E.L.D. for decades. The Infinity Formula has slowed his aging considerably. Agents are advised not to ask about the eyepatch.
notes: Classed super-soldier under the rubric's Infinity Formula rule, but the MCU version has no enhancements, so origin is contested. Record follows the original Nicholas Joseph Fury, not Nick Fury Jr.

name: Nico Minoru
caseNote: Subject is a sorceress who draws the Staff of One from her body when she bleeds, and is generally accepted as leader of the Runaways. Her parents were dark wizards in the Pride. The family business was declined.
notes: Lyrica Okano played her in Hulu's Runaways, a Marvel Television series that does not count toward mcu.

name: Night Nurse
caseNote: Subject is a trained nurse who treats superheroes and others who cannot visit a hospital. Is not herself superpowered. Agents are advised she keeps no records.
notes: Candidate resolves to Linda Carter; debut as Linda Carter (1961-09) vs as Night Nurse (Night Nurse #1, 1972-11 or Daredevil #58). Christine Palmer in Doctor Strange is a different character.

name: Night Thrasher
caseNote: Subject is an unpowered armored vigilante who founded the New Warriors and financed them through his family's foundation. He rides a skateboard into combat. Agents are advised it is not a toy.
notes: This entry is Dwayne Taylor; his brother Donyell later took the name. He uses armor and gadgets but has no powers, so origin is trained.

name: Nightcrawler
caseNote: Subject teleports short distances, leaving behind a puff of brimstone-scented smoke. A devout Catholic, former circus acrobat and veteran of the X-Men and Excalibur. Agents are advised to ventilate the room.
notes: Alan Cumming's MCU appearance is in Avengers: Doomsday (Dec 2026), after the cutoff, so mcu is false.

name: Nighthawk (Kyle Richmond)
caseNote: Subject is a wealthy heir who drank an alchemy serum for strength at night. Has served as a villain, as a Defender and as a Thunderbolt. Agents are advised that his loyalties vary by decade.
notes: Origin mutate (serum) vs trained is arguable; alignment villain/antihero/hero. Squadron Supreme counted in otherTeams because the Earth-616 version was a simulacrum.

name: Nightmare
caseNote: Subject is a demon ruler of the Dream Dimension who feeds on fear. A long-running foe of Doctor Strange. Agents are advised to log all sleep disturbances.

name: Nikki Gold
caseNote: Subject is a 31st-century Mercurian rescued by the Guardians of the Galaxy from an abandoned spacecraft. Flames radiating from her scalp double as a weapon. Agents are advised to keep extinguishers within reach.
notes: Mercurians are genetically engineered descendants of human colonists, classed as alien. Her Avengers status was honorary during the Korvac Saga and is left out.

name: Northstar
caseNote: Subject flies at superhuman speed and generates light when holding hands with his twin sister, Aurora. Founding member of Alpha Flight and one of the first openly gay superheroes in American comics. Agents should note he is also a world-class skier.
notes: The infobox's Hydra affiliation is omitted because he served only while brainwashed.

name: Nova (Frankie Raye)
caseNote: Subject is a former girlfriend of Johnny Storm who became herald of Galactus. Wields the Power Cosmic and sometimes uses the name Nova. Agents are advised not to confuse her with the Nova Corps.
notes: Not in the MCU: Nova Prime and Nova Corps characters in Guardians films are other characters. Origin cosmic (Power Cosmic); initially acquired fire powers via an experimental process.

name: Nova (Richard Rider)
caseNote: Subject is Richard Rider, an Earth teenager who became Nova by inheriting a helmet from Rhomann Dey. Founded the New Warriors and served as Nova Prime. Agents are advised to ask for the helmet back.
notes: Origin: cosmic (Nova Force) vs tech (helmet).

name: Nova (Sam Alexander)
caseNote: Subject is a teenager who inherited a Nova helmet from his father. Served in the Nova Corps and the New Warriors. Agents are advised not to ask who Nova is.
notes: Origin: cosmic vs tech. Infobox debut Marvel Point One #1 (Nov 2011); Nova #1 is his first full appearance.

name: Odin
caseNote: Subject is the All-Father, ruler of Asgard and father of Thor. Sacrificed his right eye to Mimir in exchange for wisdom. Subject is unavailable for 24 hours each year during the Odinsleep.
notes: First mentioned in Journey into Mystery #85 (Oct 1962); the infobox gives #86 as his first appearance. His place in the prehistoric Avengers of 1,000,000 BC is kept out of the avengers id.

name: Okoye
caseNote: Subject is the head of the Dora Milaje, Wakanda's elite guard, and a master of spear combat. Has served with the Avengers. Not to be trifled with, or wigged.

name: Omega Red
caseNote: Subject is a Russian super-soldier with carbonadium tentacles that drain life force. Has repeatedly fought Wolverine. Agents are advised not to shake hands.
notes: Origin mutant (Wikipedia: human mutant) vs mutate (Soviet experiment).

name: Onslaught
caseNote: Subject is a psionic entity born of the dark halves of two mutants. Threatened to end the world. Agents are advised not to merge their minds with anyone.
notes: Origin: psionic entity mutant (Wikipedia) vs cosmic/other. Aliases exclude Xavier and Magneto.

name: Overdrive
debutIssue: Free Comic Book Day: The Amazing Spider-Man #1
caseNote: Subject is a getaway driver who can turn any vehicle into a high-powered one. Has worked for Mister Negative and served in Boomerang's Sinister Six. Agents are advised to note his license plate.
notes: His infobox says 'Free Comic Book Day: Spider-Man (July 2007)', but the article's publication history and Mister Negative's article date this same 'Swing Shift' issue to May 2007. Origin set to tech because his vehicle-modifying power works through nanites.

name: Paladin
caseNote: Subject is a mercenary who sells his services to whomever pays. Has worked with Heroes for Hire and the Thunderbolts. Agents are advised to check the invoice.
notes: Todd Stashwick appears as Paladin in VisionQuest (2026-10-13). Alignment antihero vs hero is arguable.

name: Patriot (Eli Bradley)
mcuFirst: The Falcon and the Winter Soldier
caseNote: Subject is the grandson of Isaiah Bradley and a founding member of the Young Avengers. His first powers came from an illegal street drug; his later ones from a transfusion of his grandfather's blood. The first method is not endorsed.
notes: Eli first faked powers with Mutant Growth Hormone; a transfusion from Isaiah Bradley later gave him real Super-Soldier abilities. In the MCU he appears as civilian Eli Bradley (Elijah Richardson), not as Patriot.

name: Peggy Carter
caseNote: Subject fought with the French Resistance during World War II and later served S.H.I.E.L.D. for many years. Was Captain America's wartime sweetheart. Agents are reminded she was doing this job before most of them were born.
notes: Wikipedia's infobox lists her first, unnamed and obscured, in Tales of Suspense #75 (March 1966); she was first named in 1973. The infobox's Avengers link was a support-staff role and is omitted; the Strategic Scientific Reserve is her MCU agency.

name: Pepper Potts
caseNote: Subject began as Tony Stark's secretary and has since helped run his company. Has taken the field in powered armor of her own. Subject's patience with Mr. Stark is considered her greatest power.
notes: Origin is tech for the Rescue armor and the chest-mounted device that leads Wikipedia to class her as a cyborg. The Avengers entry in her infobox is not supported by the comics text, so it is left out.

name: Phastos
caseNote: Subject is the Eternal technologist who forged weapons for gods and mortals. Associated with the Greek god Hephaestus. Warranty on the weapons has long expired.
notes: Infobox lists vol. 2 #1; the character may have earlier mentions, but the infobox is followed.

name: Phil Coulson
caseNote: Subject is a S.H.I.E.L.D. agent first encountered on the Iron Man case. Noted for composure under fire and a prized set of vintage Captain America trading cards. Reports of Subject's death have repeatedly proven unreliable.
notes: Created for the 2008 Iron Man film; his comics debut is Battle Scars #6 (April 2012). Classed as a hero overall, though the comics version later served Mephisto, led the Squadron Supreme of America and was the main villain of Heroes Reborn (2021).

name: Phyla-Vell
caseNote: Subject is the daughter of Mar-Vell, a Titanian-Kree hybrid who carried the Quantum Bands and later the title Martyr. Agents are advised that names are being recycled.
notes: Origin: Titanian/Kree alien vs cosmic (Quantum Bands). Teams based on infobox listing Guardians; Annihilators from Annihilation: Conquest.

name: Pip the Troll
caseNote: Subject is a Laxidazian prince turned troll by mutagenic ale. Has served with the Infinity Watch and X-Factor Investigations, and once kept the Space Gem between his toes. Agents are advised to inspect all footwear.
notes: The infobox dates Strange Tales #179 to February 1975, but the Adam Warlock article cites it as April 1975 (#178 was February). Best known for the Infinity Watch; X-Factor Investigations is his only membership on the TEAMS list. He appears in Eternals as a CGI character voiced by Patton Oswalt.

name: Pixie
caseNote: Subject is a British mutant who teleports in a burst of pixie dust and wields a magical soulsword. Rose from the student body to the X-Men. Agents are advised to wear a jacket against the sparkles.
notes: Origin mutant with magic-derived soulsword; mutant used as her teleportation is her X-gene power.

name: Polaris
caseNote: Subject controls magnetism and is known for her green hair. Daughter of Magneto and a longtime member of X-Factor. Agents are advised to remove all metal before the interview.
notes: Primary team is X-Factor (government X-Factor, leader of All-New X-Factor, Krakoa-era X-Factor), though she has also served on X-Men rosters. Emma Dumont's role in The Gifted is Fox TV, not MCU.

name: Prodigy (David Alleyne)
caseNote: Subject is a mutant who absorbed the knowledge and skills of those around him, and kept what he had learned after losing his powers on M-Day. He later served with the Young Avengers and X-Factor. This office envies his study habits.
notes: Here new-mutants means Danielle Moonstar's 2003 New Mutants training squad at the Xavier Institute. He lost his powers on M-Day and got them back through Krakoa's resurrection protocols.

name: Professor X
mcuFirst: Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness
caseNote: Subject is among the world's most powerful telepaths and founded the X-Men at his school in Westchester, New York. Has relied on a wheelchair for much of his career. Agents are advised that he already knows why they called.
notes: Patrick Stewart played Earth-838's Charles Xavier in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness; his Avengers: Doomsday return (Dec 2026) is after the cutoff. 'Onslaught' is omitted as an alias because Onslaught is a separate game character.

name: Proteus
caseNote: Subject is a reality-warping mutant whose body is unstable. Son of Moira MacTaggert. Agents are advised not to ask about his mother.

name: Prowler (Hobie Brown)
caseNote: Subject is an inventor who built the Prowler gear after being fired from his window-washing job and first used it as a thief. Spider-Man unmasked him and advised him to rethink his life; he has been an ally since. Agents should not underestimate window washers.
notes: Not the MCU Prowler (Aaron Davis) or Spider-Punk, the Earth-138 Hobie Brown; this Hobie Brown has never appeared in live action, so players are likely to confuse the entries.

name: Proxima Midnight
caseNote: Subject is a Black Order enforcer armed with a spear forged from a star that homes in on its target. Married to fellow Order member Corvus Glaive. Agents should not assume they can outrun the spear.
notes: Wikipedia now covers her in a list entry with no infobox. The debut comes from the entry text (New Avengers #8, September 2013), which matches the infobox of the 2023 version of her article.

name: Psycho-Man
caseNote: Subject is a Micronian ruler who controls emotions with a handheld device. Operates from the Microverse and has repeatedly targeted the Fantastic Four. Agents are advised to remain calm; he will not allow it.
notes: Origin contested: alien (Micronian) vs tech (emotion-control technology).

name: Psylocke (Betsy Braddock)
caseNote: Subject is a British telepath able to focus her power into a psychic knife. Twin sister of Captain Britain, a title she later took on herself, and a longtime member of the X-Men and X-Force. Agents are advised not to think too loudly.
notes: Her MCU credit is an uncredited alternate-timeline Psylocke (Ayesha Hussain) in Deadpool & Wolverine, listed in Wikipedia's Betsy Braddock in other media article. 'Captain Britain' is omitted as an alias because it belongs primarily to Brian Braddock.

name: Puma
caseNote: Subject is Thomas Fireheart, a mercenary and CEO bred by his tribe to be a perfect warrior. Transforms into an anthropomorphic mountain lion. Once bought the Daily Bugle to repay a debt of honor.
notes: Alignment is contested: he began as an assassin hired to kill Spider-Man, later became an ally and Outlaws member, and has slipped back into mercenary villainy. His powers come from genetic engineering combined with tribal mysticism; origin set to magic.

name: Punisher
caseNote: Subject is a former Marine who wages a lethal war on crime after his family was killed. Possesses no superhuman powers, only a large inventory. Agents are advised not to ask about the skull.
notes: Thunderbolts and Savage Avengers memberships were brief and left out.

name: Puppet Master
caseNote: Subject is a sculptor who controls people through clay figures of radioactive material. Stepfather of Alicia Masters. Agents are advised not to sit for portraits.
notes: Origin contested: tech (radioactive clay) vs mutate.

name: Purple Man
caseNote: Subject is a spy whose skin turned purple after a chemical accident and who compels obedience. Menaced Daredevil and Jessica Jones. Agents are advised to decline any request politely worded as an order.
notes: Netflix Jessica Jones does not count toward mcu.

name: Pyro
caseNote: Subject controls flame and cannot create it. Has served the Brotherhood and Freedom Force. Agents are advised to bring a lighter.
notes: Alignment villain; occasionally hero-adjacent.

name: Quake
caseNote: Subject generates powerful vibrations and once directed S.H.I.E.L.D. Also led the Secret Warriors. Agents are advised not to stand on shaky ground.
notes: Live-action portrayal was in ABC Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D., which does not count.

name: Quasar
caseNote: Subject is Wendell Vaughn, a former security agent who wears the Quantum Bands. Served with the Avengers as Protector of the Universe. Agents are advised not to borrow his jewelry.
notes: Resolved infobox was wrong; used the Quasar article. Wendell Vaughn Quasar debut #234; Marvel Boy debut Captain America #217 (1978-01). Other Quasars: Phyla-Vell, Richard Rider.

name: Quentin Quire
caseNote: Subject is an Omega-level telepath and telekinetic from the Xavier Institute. Led a student uprising before turning into a Phoenix host. Agents are advised not to dismiss him.
notes: Alignment is contested between antihero and villain early on, hero later.

name: Quicksilver
caseNote: Subject moves at superhuman speed and is the twin brother of the Scarlet Witch. Former Brotherhood of Mutants member who later served with the Avengers and X-Factor. Patience is not among his documented abilities.
notes: Origin contested: portrayed as Magneto's mutant son for decades, but a 2015 retcon (and the MCU) attribute his powers to experiments; classed mutate.

name: Rachel Summers
caseNote: Subject is a telepath and telekinetic from a dystopian future, the daughter of Cyclops and Jean Grey. Has hosted the Phoenix Force and served with the X-Men and Excalibur. Agents are advised not to ask how the future turns out.
notes: 'Phoenix' and 'Marvel Girl', which she has also used, are omitted as aliases because they belong primarily to Jean Grey.

name: Radioactive Man
caseNote: Subject is a Chinese nuclear physicist who gained radiation powers. Has served as a villain and a Thunderbolt. Agents are advised to bring lead-lined clothing.
notes: Infobox lists two bearers; Chen Lu is the original.

name: Ravonna Renslayer
caseNote: Subject is a Time Variance Authority officer who has served, and later opposed, powerful time-traveling conquerors. Comics history includes a spell as Terminatrix. Agents are advised that her loyalties are subject to change without notice.
notes: Alignment (villain vs antihero) and primary team (TVA is MCU-derived) are contested.

name: Red Guardian
caseNote: Subject is a former Soviet test pilot and KGB agent trained as his nation's answer to Captain America. Was once married to the Black Widow. His throwing disc doubles as a belt buckle.
notes: Record follows Alexei Shostakov, the MCU's Red Guardian, in a mantle with several holders. Comics Alexei has no superhuman powers, but MCU tie-in material presents him as a Soviet super-soldier, so origin is contested.

name: Red Hulk
caseNote: Subject is a career general who spent years hunting the Hulk before becoming a red gamma giant himself. Radiates heat, absorbs energy, and has led the Thunderbolts. The irony has been noted for the record.
notes: Record treats Red Hulk as Thaddeus Ross, so debut and mcuFirst follow Ross (Wikipedia's Red Hulk mantle article has no infobox). As Red Hulk he debuted in Hulk vol. 2 #1 (2008) and first appeared on screen in Captain America: Brave New World (2025).

name: Red She-Hulk
caseNote: Subject is a general's daughter and Bruce Banner's wife who was transformed by gamma radiation into a red-skinned powerhouse. Has served with the Defenders. Family gatherings are considered high-risk.
notes: Wikipedia's Red She-Hulk redirects to Betty Ross, so debut and MCU follow Betty (the infobox says March 1962, but The Incredible Hulk #1 is cover-dated May 1962). She first became Red She-Hulk in Hulk vol. 2 #15 (September 2009) and has never appeared in that form in live action.

name: Red Skull
caseNote: Subject is a Nazi operative with a face like a crimson skull and the archenemy of Captain America. Has commanded Hydra and favors a poison known as the dust of death. Agents are advised to decline all handshakes.
notes: Origin is contested: the comics Johann Shmidt is unpowered for most of his history, but super-soldier fits the MCU's early Super-Soldier Serum and his comics years in a Super-Soldier-derived clone body. Wikipedia dates the Red Skull to Captain America Comics #1 (1941), where George Maxon wore the identity.

name: Rhino
caseNote: Subject is Aleksei Sytsevich, a low-ranking Russian mobster who volunteered for chemical and radiation treatments. They left him with superhuman strength and a rhinoceros-shaped polymer suit. Agents are advised to step aside.
notes: Thunderbolts membership comes from Wilson Fisk's teams in King in Black and Devil's Reign. His live-action films (The Amazing Spider-Man 2, Kraven the Hunter) are Sony productions, not MCU.

name: Rick Jones
caseNote: Subject is a teenager who was saved by Bruce Banner during a gamma test. Has been Captain America's sidekick and the Hulk's friend. Agents are advised to keep distance from gamma tests.
notes: Origin contested: gamma mutate vs other enhancements.

name: Rictor
caseNote: Subject is a Mexican mutant who generates seismic vibrations. Has served with X-Factor and X-Force. Agents are advised to hold the tremors until after the meeting.
notes: Infobox alliances empty; teams taken from article body.

name: Rocket Raccoon
caseNote: Subject is a raccoon engineered into a sapient soldier on the planet Halfworld. Pilot, tinkerer and weapons specialist of the Guardians. Agents are advised not to call him a rodent.

name: Rocket Racer
caseNote: Subject is Robert Farrell, a Brooklyn native and eldest of seven children who rides a self-built rocket skateboard. Began as a thief but reformed after run-ins with Spider-Man. Agents are advised he does not stay off the sidewalk.
notes: He debuted as a thief but reformed after early clashes with Spider-Man and later trained with the Initiative and Avengers Academy, so he is set to hero. He has no standalone Wikipedia article.

name: Rockslide
caseNote: Subject is a mutant who forms a rock body from surrounding earth and can reassemble after being shattered. He trained at the Xavier Institute and served with the Young X-Men. Demolition requests should be routed through proper channels.
notes: His teams were Xavier Institute student squads with no TEAMS id, and he never served on an X-Men main roster, so primaryTeam is none.

name: Rogue
caseNote: Subject absorbs the memories and abilities of anyone she touches. Formerly of the Brotherhood of Evil Mutants, later a mainstay of the X-Men and the Avengers Unity Squad. Handshakes are not recommended.
notes: She began as a Brotherhood villain before joining the X-Men, but is classified hero overall. Her surname is unrevealed in canon, and Inde Navarrette's casting is for the 2028 X-Men film.

name: Ronan the Accuser
caseNote: Subject is the Kree Empire's chief enforcer, wielding the Universal Weapon. Has opposed the Fantastic Four, Avengers and Guardians. Agents are advised that the hammer is not for sale.

name: Sabretooth
caseNote: Subject is a feral mutant with claws, enhanced senses and a healing factor. Has hunted Wolverine for decades. Agents are advised that a polite request to stop is not effective.
notes: Appears in Deadpool & Wolverine as a returning Fox-film actor (Tyler Mane); cameo counts per rubric.

name: Sandman
caseNote: Subject is career criminal William Baker, alias Flint Marko, whose body turned to sand after exposure to irradiated sand at a nuclear test site. A founding member of both the Sinister Six and the Frightful Four. Agents should check their shoes after any encounter.
notes: Wikipedia notes he later became an antihero (Avengers reserve, Wild Pack, Outlaws), but he has spent most of his history as a villain; the brief Avengers reserve stint is not counted. His birth name is William Baker; Flint Marko is an alias.

name: Satana
caseNote: Subject is a succubus and the daughter of Marduk Kurios. Has fought Doctor Strange and joined several teams of villains. Agents are advised to count their souls after meeting.
notes: Infobox lists Vampire Tales #2; alignment fluctuates between hero and villain.

name: Sauron
caseNote: Subject is a physician transformed into a pterodactyl creature that feeds on mutants. Believes the Savage Land should be his. Agents are advised to bring a guide.
notes: Origin mutate vs mutant. Mentions in MCU snippet refer to Tolkien's Sauron.

name: Scarlet Spider (Ben Reilly)
caseNote: Subject is a clone of Peter Parker grown by the Jackal, who named himself after Uncle Ben and Aunt May's maiden name. Took over as Spider-Man in the mid-1990s while both men believed Parker was the clone. The matter has since been settled; agents should not reopen it.
notes: Debut uses the 1975 clone listed first in the infobox; he returned as Ben Reilly/Scarlet Spider in 1994. Wikipedia calls him a superhero, but he has had villainous turns as the Jackal and Chasm, and his New Warriors stint was brief.

name: Scarlet Witch
caseNote: Subject wields chaos magic capable of altering reality. Former Brotherhood of Mutants member who joined the Avengers in 1965 and later married the Vision. Probability is not to be relied upon in her presence.
notes: Origin contested: introduced as a mutant, retconned in 2015 as a High Evolutionary experiment subject, and now written (as in the MCU) as a chaos-magic witch; classed magic. MCU debut is the Winter Soldier mid-credits scene.

name: Scorpion
caseNote: Subject is Mac Gargan, a private investigator hired by J. Jonah Jameson, who then funded an untested procedure to make him a match for Spider-Man. It granted scorpion-like abilities and a mechanical tail but damaged his mind. Mr. Jameson's research funding is under review.
notes: Debut uses Mac Gargan's first appearance (ASM #19, December 1964); he became the Scorpion in ASM #20 (January 1965). His Dark Avengers and Thunderbolts tenures were as Venom, and he first appears as the Scorpion on screen in Brand New Day (2026).

name: Scream
caseNote: Subject is Donna Diego, a Life Foundation volunteer bonded to one of five symbiotes forcibly spawned from Venom. Uses her prehensile hair as a weapon. Agents are advised that the codename is descriptive.
notes: The Scream symbiote has had several hosts; this record follows the original, Donna Diego.

name: Sebastian Shaw
caseNote: Subject is an industrialist who absorbs kinetic energy and grows stronger. Has served as Black King of the Hellfire Club. Agents are advised not to hit Subject.

name: Selene
caseNote: Subject is an immortal who has lived for millennia and feeds on life force. Has led the Hellfire Club. Agents are advised to avoid inviting Subject to dinner.
notes: Origin mutant (Wikipedia) vs magic (psychic vampire, sorcery).

name: Sentry
caseNote: Subject derives the power of a million exploding suns from an experimental serum. Has served with the New Avengers and the Dark Avengers. A dark counterpart called the Void is attached to his file and should not be engaged.
notes: Infobox gives only the year; the article's citations date the original miniseries September 2000 to January 2001. 'World Breaker' left out of aliases because it belongs primarily to Hulk.

name: Sersi
caseNote: Subject is an Eternal able to transmute matter at will. Has served with the Avengers and Heroes for Hire. Her hobbies include turning inconvenient objects into other inconvenient objects.
notes: Infobox lists earlier appearances as Circe (Venus #9, 1950; Strange Tales #109, 1963); the 1976 debut as Sersi is used since the character as played is Sersi.

name: Shang-Chi
mcuFirst: Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings
caseNote: Subject is a martial arts master and son of Fu Manchu in his original comics. Rejected his father's criminal empire. Agents are advised that he is, in fact, not Bruce Lee.

name: Shanna the She-Devil
caseNote: Subject is a jungle adventurer and wife of Ka-Zar. Raised in the wild. Agents are advised to leave the animals alone.
notes: Origin per infobox 'human mutate'; could also be trained.

name: Sharon Carter
caseNote: Subject is a veteran S.H.I.E.L.D. field agent known by a numbered code name. A longtime partner of Captain America and kin to a celebrated World War II heroine. Family reunions are classified.
notes: Avengers membership is via the 2010 Secret Avengers and Thunderbolts via Bucky Barnes's 2023 team. The MCU version is revealed as the Power Broker in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, but she is a hero across her history.

name: Shatterstar
caseNote: Subject is a gladiator from Mojoworld, bred to fight with twin swords. Is a veteran of X-Force and a part of the Krakoan era X-Men. Agents are advised not to call him by his gladiator name at the dinner table.
notes: Alien (Mojoworld, genetically engineered) vs mutant. MCU: Lewis Tan as Rusty / Shatterstar in Deadpool & Wolverine (cameo as an X-Force member). 'Ben Russell' is an Earth alias.

name: She-Hulk
caseNote: Subject is an attorney who gained gamma-powered strength from an emergency blood transfusion from her cousin, Bruce Banner. Has served with the Avengers and the Fantastic Four. Known to address the reader directly; agents should not be alarmed.
notes: Infobox lists November 1979 (on-sale date); the February 1980 cover date is used per rubric.

name: Shocker
caseNote: Subject is Herman Schultz, a self-taught engineer who built vibro-shock gauntlets after being jailed and used them to escape. Wears a foam-lined suit to absorb the vibrations. Agents should stand well back.
notes: Two men were the Shocker in Homecoming (Jackson Brice, then Herman Schultz played by Bokeem Woodbine); this entry is Schultz.

name: Shriek
caseNote: Subject is a mutant whose powers were awakened by exposure to Cloak's Darkforce. Projects sonic blasts and draws out the darkness in others. Agents are advised she has no indoor voice.

name: Shuma-Gorath
caseNote: Subject is a tentacled extradimensional entity of enormous power. Has repeatedly sought to conquer Earth. Agents are advised not to make eye contact with the eye.
notes: Cosmic is a defensible origin; magic chosen under the mystic-entities rule.

name: Shuri
caseNote: Subject is the princess of Wakanda, a master inventor, and a former Black Panther. Heart-shaped herb enhances her abilities. Her devices are not available for loan.
notes: Origin contested: mutate (heart-shaped herb) vs trained.

name: Sif
caseNote: Subject is a leading Asgardian warrior and Thor's companion since childhood. Born with golden hair, which turned black after Loki cut it and replaced it with dwarf-made hair. Loki is barred from the salon.

name: Silk
caseNote: Subject was bitten by the same radioactive spider as Peter Parker, then spent years locked in a facility for her own protection. Shoots webbing from her fingertips and has a danger sense stronger than Parker's. Agents should not offer to lock any doors for her.
notes: MCU status rests on Cindy Moon appearing as Peter's classmate (Tiffany Espensen) from Homecoming on, never as Silk. Wikipedia lists April 2014 (on-sale month) for the cameo; the issue's cover date is June 2014, and her full appearance is #4.

name: Silver Sable
caseNote: Subject is a Symkarian mercenary who leads the Wild Pack and runs Silver Sable International, which hunts war criminals for a fee. Has no superhuman powers and has been both ally and opponent to Spider-Man. Agents should request a quote in advance.
notes: Wikipedia gives her real name as Silvija Sablinova (older sources: Silver Sablinova). The infobox lists Heroes for Hire, but the article only shows her fighting them, so it is omitted.

name: Silver Samurai
caseNote: Subject is an armored swordsman who generates a tachyon edge. Has served Japan's criminal underworld. Agents are advised to bring a thicker blade.
notes: Two characters use the name; Kenuichio Harada (1974) used per infobox. Origin mutant vs tech (armor).

name: Silver Surfer
caseNote: Subject is a former scientist of Zenn-La who became Galactus's herald to save his world. Rides a board and wields the Power Cosmic. Agents should note that the paint is not removable.
notes: Comics Surfer is Norrin Radd (male); First Steps features Shalla-Bal (Julia Garner) as the Silver Surfer, which still counts for mcu. Shalla-Bal is listed as an alias since players may type it.

name: Silvermane
caseNote: Subject is a Maggia don nicknamed for his near-white hair. Has pursued immortality through a youth formula and, later, a cyborg body. Agents are advised that retirement is not in his plans.
notes: Origin set to tech for his cyborg bodies; he began as an unpowered elderly mob boss relying on a youth formula. Hydra comes from his infobox (alias 'Supreme Hydra') and Hydra's former-member list, though the text only says he sought to lead Hydra. 'Supreme Hydra' is left out of aliases because it belongs mainly to Baron Strucker.

name: Sin
caseNote: Subject is the daughter of the Red Skull and a leader of the Serpent Squad. Has acted as head of Hydra. Agents are advised that family gatherings are not safe.
notes: MCU snippets were unrelated uses of the word sin. Origin per infobox.

name: Siryn
caseNote: Subject is a sonic-scream mutant, the daughter of Banshee, with a famous temper. Has served on X-Factor Investigations and X-Force. Agents are advised against asking her to keep it down.
notes: Real name Theresa Cassidy (Theresa Maeve Rourke Cassidy in the article).

name: Skaar
caseNote: Subject is the son of the Hulk, born on the planet Sakaar. Inherited Hulk's strength and anger. Agents are advised to avoid family reunions.
notes: Origin contested between mutate (gamma) and alien (Sakaaran). Appears in She-Hulk via motion capture.

name: Songbird
caseNote: Subject is a former criminal who uses sonic powers. Has served on the Thunderbolts and the Avengers. Agents are advised to bring ear protection.
notes: Alignment hero vs antihero contested; origin per infobox.

name: Speed
debutIssue: The Vision and the Scarlet Witch vol. 2 #12
caseNote: Subject is a mutant speedster and the twin brother of Wiccan. The Young Avengers found him held in a juvenile facility after he reportedly vaporized his school. Interviews should be brief; Subject will not wait.
notes: Wikipedia's infobox lists the infant Thomas Maximoff's first appearance (Vision and the Scarlet Witch #12, Sept 1986), while Tommy Shepherd debuted in Young Avengers #10 (Mar 2006). The infobox also lists the Champions, but the article describes no such membership.

name: Speedball
caseNote: Subject was struck by extradimensional energy at a research lab, leaving him wrapped in bouncing kinetic force fields. A founding New Warrior, he later operated as Penance. The spiked suit is no longer required.
notes: Wikipedia's infobox says 'January 1988', but the annual has no cover month and other references date it to later in 1988, so debutDate gives the year only. His Thunderbolts membership was as Penance.

name: Spider-Girl (Anya Corazon)
caseNote: Subject was mortally wounded in a clash between two mystical clans and saved by a Spider Society ritual that granted her spider-powers. Operated as Araña before taking the Spider-Girl name. The Spider Society is not a book club.
notes: Origin is contested: her first powers came from a Spider Society mystical ritual, while her later spider-powers came from the Jackal's Spider-Island virus; Wikipedia classes her as human mutate. Her only live-action role is in Sony's Madame Web (2024), not MCU.

name: Spider-Girl (Mayday Parker)
caseNote: Subject is the teenage daughter of Peter Parker and Mary Jane Watson in the alternate MC2 reality. Inherited her father's spider-powers and became Spider-Girl, at first hindered and then helped by her worried parents. Curfew violations are presumed.
notes: Her powers are inherited from Peter Parker rather than gained in an accident; mutate follows Wikipedia's 'human mutate'. Her reserve status with MC2's A-Next is not counted as Avengers membership.

name: Spider-Gwen
caseNote: Subject is the Gwen Stacy of Earth-65, where she, not Peter Parker, was bitten by the radioactive spider. Has operated as Spider-Woman and Ghost-Spider and drums for a band called the Mary Janes. Agents should confirm which Gwen Stacy they are addressing.
notes: Wikipedia's infobox gives September 2014, the on-sale month; CGC lists the November 2014 cover date. Her Spider-Woman codename is left out of aliases because it belongs to Jessica Drew.

name: Spider-Ham
debutIssue: Marvel Tails Starring Peter Porker, the Spectacular Spider-Ham #1
caseNote: Subject was born a spider and was bitten by scientist May Porker after she irradiated herself with an atomic-powered hairdryer, turning him into an anthropomorphic pig with spider-powers. Agents are reminded that he is, in fact, a pig.

name: Spider-Man (Miles Morales)
caseNote: Subject was bitten by a genetically engineered spider and took up the Spider-Man name after the apparent death of his universe's Peter Parker. Can turn invisible and deliver a paralyzing 'venom strike'. Agents should not assume there is only one Spider-Man.
notes: Primary team is the Champions (founding member, longest tenure) rather than the All-New, All-Different Avengers; in the MCU he is only alluded to, never shown. Wikipedia's August 2011 is the on-sale month (released 3 August 2011); dealer listings suggest an October 2011 cover date that I could not confirm from a source I could open.

name: Spider-Man (Peter Parker)
caseNote: Subject gained spider-like abilities after a radioactive spider bit him at a science exhibit. Has sold photographs of himself to the Daily Bugle, which routinely labels him a menace. Agents are advised not to ask who took the pictures.
notes: Teams follow the Wikipedia infobox: fantastic-four reflects his 2011 Future Foundation/FF membership and web-warriors the Spider-Army of the Spider-Verse events.

name: Spider-Man 2099
caseNote: Subject is Miguel O'Hara, a geneticist of the year 2099 whose DNA was half-rewritten with spider genes in an accident at Alchemax. Has talons, venomous fangs and the ability to see in darkness. Reports he files are dated 2099; this is not a clerical error.
notes: Debut is the preview in ASM #365; his first full appearance is Spider-Man 2099 #1 (November 1992). The infobox lists only Exiles and Alchemax; web-warriors reflects his Spider-Army role in the 2014 Spider-Verse event.

name: Spider-Slayer (Alistair Smythe)
caseNote: Subject is the son of Spencer Smythe and continues the family business of building robots to destroy Spider-Man. Wears a bio-organic carapace that restored his ability to walk. Agents are advised the business has one target.
notes: His only live-action role is in Sony's The Amazing Spider-Man 2, which does not count for the MCU.

name: Spider-Woman (Jessica Drew)
caseNote: Subject gained spider-like powers through her scientist father's experiments. Recruited by Hydra before defecting, she later served S.H.I.E.L.D. and S.W.O.R.D. Her pheromones may impair agents' judgment.
notes: A 2006 retcon changed her spider-blood serum origin to a spider-DNA laser experiment; both are mutate. No live-action MCU appearance (her only film role is the animated, Sony-made Across the Spider-Verse).

name: Spiral
caseNote: Subject is a six-armed sorceress who serves Mojo. Has opposed and later aided the X-Men. Agents are advised not to count her hands.
notes: Infobox says human mutate; she is a sorcerer in practice. Alignment contested.

name: Spot
caseNote: Subject is a scientist who, while working for the Kingpin, tried to replicate Cloak's teleportation and ended up covered in portals. Can reach through his spots to strike from anywhere. Agents are advised not to treat him as a villain of the week.
notes: Debut uses the infobox's listing of his appearance as an unnamed man in #97; he first appeared as the Spot in #98 (January 1985). Wikipedia spells his first name inconsistently (Jonathon/Johnathon), so the common spelling Jonathan is used and the variants are aliases.

name: Sprite
caseNote: Subject is an Eternal who appears as a child and has the power to create illusions. Known as a prankster and trickster. Subject has been appearing younger than agents for several thousand years.
notes: Resolved infobox was wrong (Ora Serrata); debut and details from the Sprite (Eternal) article and search. Gender contested: male in comics, female in the MCU.

name: Squirrel Girl
caseNote: Subject has the combined powers of squirrel and girl, including a prehensile tail and fluency in squirrel. In her first recorded engagement she helped Iron Man defeat Doctor Doom. Agents should not underestimate the squirrels.
notes: Wikipedia calls her a human mutate: her squirrel traits have no stated cause, and later stories say she is not a mutant, so origin is debatable. The cover date is 'Winter 1991', so no month is given; primary team is the Great Lakes Avengers, though she later served on the New Avengers and U.S.Avengers.

name: Star-Lord
caseNote: Subject is a half-human, half-alien outlaw abducted from Earth as a child. Leads the Guardians of the Galaxy and has briefly served in the Nova Corps. Agents are advised to confiscate the cassette player.
notes: Half-Spartoi heritage; origin could be argued as mutate or alien. Infobox gives Marvel Preview #4 as overall debut (Earth-616 debut Thanos #8, 2004).

name: Starfox
caseNote: Subject is Eros of Titan, brother of Thanos, a member of the Avengers and Eternals who can influence emotions. Appears briefly in a film mid-credits scene. Agents are advised to remain unmoved.

name: Starhawk
caseNote: Subject is a 31st-century hero fated to relive his own life repeatedly, and calls himself the One Who Knows. Shares a long, strained history with his adoptive sister Aleta. Agents should assume Subject has read this memo before.
notes: Wikipedia's lead calls him an antihero, but he is filed as a superhero. His powers come from the Arcturan Hawk God, so origin is set to cosmic. Ravagers is an MCU-only affiliation; the 1969 Guardians were only honorary Avengers (Korvac Saga), so that is left out.

name: Stature
caseNote: Subject is the daughter of Scott Lang and a size-changing member of the Young Avengers. Her abilities stem from years of secretly taking her father's Pym Particles. Agents are reminded to secure their Pym Particles.
notes: The debut is Cassie Lang's first appearance as a child; she first became Stature in Young Avengers #6. In the comics her powers come from Pym Particle exposure (mutate), while the MCU version uses a suit.

name: Stegron
caseNote: Subject is a former S.H.I.E.L.D. agent who studied Savage Land dinosaur DNA with Curt Connors, then injected himself with it. Now transforms into a bipedal stegosaurus that can command dinosaurs. Agents are advised to secure all museum fossils.

name: Stick
caseNote: Subject is a blind martial arts master who trained Daredevil. Leads the Chaste against the Hand. Agents are advised that his teaching methods are bluntly practical.
notes: Alignment hero vs antihero is arguable. Netflix appearances do not count.

name: Storm
caseNote: Subject commands weather on a planetary scale and has led the X-Men in the field. Has also served with the Avengers and the Fantastic Four, and reigned as Queen of Wakanda. Agents are advised not to schedule picnics.
notes: No live-action MCU appearance by the cutoff; Maya Boyd is cast for the 2028 X-Men film. wakanda reflects her tenure as Queen of Wakanda.

name: Strong Guy
caseNote: Subject absorbs kinetic energy and rechannels it as physical strength. Has been a long-standing member of X-Factor. Agents are advised not to hit him.

name: Stryfe
caseNote: Subject is a clone of Cable, raised in a different time. Founded the Mutant Liberation Front. Agents are advised not to take sides.
notes: Real name is shared with the original (Nathan Summers), so realName left empty.

name: Sunfire
caseNote: Subject ionizes matter into superheated plasma, which also lets him fly. A Japanese mutant who quit the X-Men after a single mission in 1975 and later served with the Avengers Unity Squad. Agents are advised not to ask him for a light.
notes: He began as a nationalist antagonist and quit the X-Men after one mission, but was later elected to the Krakoa-era X-Men and served in Uncanny Avengers. Hero and x-men as primary team are judgment calls.

name: Sunspot
debutIssue: Marvel Graphic Novel #4: The New Mutants
caseNote: Subject is a Brazilian heir who absorbs solar energy for strength and heat. Has led the Avengers and taken control of A.I.M. Agents are advised that he can pay for lunch.
notes: Teams chosen from a long infobox list.

name: Super-Adaptoid
caseNote: Subject is an android capable of copying the powers of heroes it touches. Created by A.I.M. Agents are advised not to shake hands with it.
notes: Infobox debut (as Adaptoid) used.

name: Super-Skrull
caseNote: Subject is a Skrull warrior given the combined powers of the Fantastic Four. Dispatched to Earth to destroy them and later a reluctant ally. Agents will note he has all four powers and no sense of humor.
notes: Alignment contested: villain (most appearances) vs antihero (later ally of the FF).

name: Supergiant
caseNote: Subject is a Black Order telepath who seizes control of other minds. Once hijacked Black Bolt to trigger the Illuminati's hidden bombs. Agents are advised to keep their thoughts to themselves.
notes: The only founding Black Order member left out of the MCU films.

name: Supreme Intelligence
caseNote: Subject is the Kree collective consciousness serving as the empire's ruler. A computer built from the greatest Kree minds. Agents are advised to stay out of its meeting.
notes: Alignment villain (Kree ruler); neutral also arguable. Gender: other (non-person composite).

name: Surge
caseNote: Subject is a mutant who absorbs ambient electricity and must discharge it, relying on gauntlets to regulate the flow. She led the New X-Men student squad after M-Day. Visitors should ground themselves before handshakes.
notes: Here new-mutants means Danielle Moonstar's 2003 New Mutants training squad; she later led the merged New X-Men student squad.

name: Surtur
caseNote: Subject is a fire giant of Muspelheim, over 1,000 feet tall, who wields the Twilight Sword. A recurring threat to Asgard and a central figure in the prophecy of Ragnarok. Fire extinguishers are not considered an adequate response.
notes: Infobox lists a cameo in Journey into Mystery #97 (Oct 1963) and a full appearance in #99 (Dec 1963). Species is Fire Giant (deity), though he is also described as a fire demon; his MCU role is CGI with Taika Waititi's motion capture and Clancy Brown's voice.

name: Swarm
caseNote: Subject is a former Nazi scientist whose body was devoured by mutated bees, leaving his mind in command of the hive. Operates as a humanoid mass of bees. Agents with allergies should request reassignment.
notes: His infobox lists the Sinister Six, but that was a team he led in a single issue (Spider-Man and the X-Men #4), so no team is set.

name: Swordsman
caseNote: Subject is a swordsman and former circus performer who infiltrated the Avengers. Later died fighting for them. Agents are advised not to challenge him to duels.
notes: Captain Marvel snippet was an unrelated common noun. Jack Duquesne appears in Hawkeye (2021) and Daredevil: Born Again; Hawkeye was not in the match file and is based on cast knowledge, verify. Alignment contested.

name: Talos
caseNote: Subject is a Skrull shapeshifter and military leader who sometimes poses as Jonathan Richards. Appears in Marvel's cosmic conflicts. Agents are advised that everyone in the room may be him.
notes: Alignment: villain in comics, antihero/ally in MCU. mcuFirst Captain Marvel (2019).

name: Tarantula
caseNote: Subject is a former revolutionary terrorist from a small South American republic, schooled in military tactics and martial arts. Fights with envenomed spikes on the toes of his boots. Agents are advised to watch his feet.
notes: Several characters have used the name. This record follows the original, Anton Miguel Rodriquez, whom Wikipedia credits with a cameo in Spider-Man: Brand New Day (performer unidentified). Origin set to trained because the Brand Corporation mutated him into a spider-creature only in his final story.

name: Taskmaster
caseNote: Subject possesses photographic reflexes, allowing him to replicate any fighting technique after watching it. Has trained countless henchmen for a fee. Agents are advised not to demonstrate their signature moves in his presence.
notes: Origin is contested: his photographic reflexes were long presented as innate, but a later retcon credits a modified Nazi Super-Soldier Serum. The MCU Taskmaster is a woman, Antonia Dreykov (Olga Kurylenko); the Avengers entry is the Marvel NOW! Secret Avengers.

name: Terrax
caseNote: Subject is a former herald of Galactus who wields the Power Cosmic via a battle-axe. Has ruled, betrayed, and been betrayed in turn. Agents are advised against asking him to settle quietly.

name: Thane
caseNote: Subject is the son of Thanos and an Inhuman mother; Terrigenesis gave him a lethal touch and the power to encase targets in amber. Wears a containment suit supplied by Ebony Maw. Handshakes are not recommended.
notes: Titanian-Inhuman hybrid. Origin set to inhuman because his powers came from Terrigenesis. The alias Phoenix is left out because it belongs to another game character.

name: Thanos
caseNote: Subject is a warlord from Titan who once assembled the Infinity Gauntlet and erased half of all life in the universe to impress Death. Commands the Black Order. Agents are reminded that snapping is not an approved form of resource management.
notes: Eternal-Deviant hybrid, so origin is alien under the rubric. The infobox also lists the Infinity Watch, but Thanos was an ally of that team, not a member, so it is left out. Cabal membership (Namor's Cabal) comes from the Cabal article.

name: The Ancient One
caseNote: Subject is the former Sorcerer Supreme and master of Doctor Strange. Has lived for centuries in the Himalayas. Agents are advised to bring tea.
notes: Tilda Swinton plays the character in Doctor Strange (2016).

name: The Angel (Thomas Halloway)
caseNote: Subject is a masked detective and occult scholar from the Golden Age. Founding member of the All-Winners Squad. Agents are advised to leave his cape alone.

name: The Collector
caseNote: Subject is an Elder of the Universe who has spent billions of years gathering rare artifacts and living specimens. Once held an Infinity Gem without understanding what it was. Personnel are advised not to stand still near display cases.
notes: Origin set to cosmic because Elders draw their power from the Power Primordial. He is also an alien by birth.

name: The Grandmaster
caseNote: Subject is an Elder of the Universe devoted to mastering games of skill and chance. Has used the Avengers as game pieces and once challenged Death to a contest of strategy. Agents should decline all invitations to play.
notes: His MCU debut is the credits cameo in Guardians of the Galaxy Vol. 2 (May 2017), which came before Thor: Ragnarok. Squadron Sinister is listed because he created and directed that team.
