name: The Hood
caseNote: Subject is a small-time thief who acquired a demonic cloak and boots granting invisibility and the ability to walk on air. Later organized much of the costumed underworld into a single syndicate. Agents should keep an eye on empty air.
notes: The Illuminati in his infobox is the villain group he formed, separate from the heroes' Illuminati, so it is listed under otherTeams.

name: The Leader
caseNote: Subject was a menial laborer until gamma radiation turned his skin green and enlarged his cranium and intellect to superhuman levels. A longtime foe of the Hulk. Agents should not attempt to out-think Subject.
notes: mcuFirst is The Incredible Hulk (2008), where Samuel Sterns appears before his transformation; he returns as the Leader in Captain America: Brave New World. He was forced to work for Ross's Thunderbolts, so that team is omitted.

name: The Owl
caseNote: Subject is a former financier who used a serum to gain strength and glide on air currents. Bald and fond of owl-themed capes. Agents are advised he did not pay his taxes.
notes: Bob Gunton's Daredevil role is Netflix and does not count.

name: The Serpent
caseNote: Subject is Cul Borson, brother of Odin and the Asgardian God of Fear, freed from an underwater prison. Broke Captain America's shield with his bare hands. His claim to be the true All-Father remains under review.
notes: Infobox dates Fear Itself #1 to April 2011 (release month); the cover date used here is June 2011, as in the article's publication history.

name: The Stranger
caseNote: Subject is a cosmic surveyor who studies other worlds and keeps specimens on a private laboratory planet. Has more than once attempted to destroy Earth. Agents are advised against volunteering for research.
notes: Alignment is contested: a detached cosmic scientist who has tried to destroy Earth but has also helped heroes; set to villain. The infobox names the debut 'Uncanny X-Men #11', the series' later title.

name: Thena
caseNote: Subject is an Eternal warrior of exceptional combat skill, associated with the Greek goddess Athena. Has served with Heroes for Hire. Agents are advised to avoid sparring.
notes: Infobox also lists earlier incarnations (Minerva, Red Raven Comics #1, 1940); Thena debut used.

name: Thing
caseNote: Subject is a former test pilot with rocky orange skin and extreme strength, the result of cosmic rays. Longest-serving muscle of the Fantastic Four. Catchphrase is on file and will not be repeated.

name: Thor
caseNote: Subject is the Asgardian God of Thunder and wielder of the enchanted hammer Mjolnir. Founding member of the Avengers who once lived as mortal physician Donald Blake. Weather forecasts in his vicinity are unreliable.
notes: Eric Masterson left out of aliases because that identity belongs primarily to Thunderstrike.

name: Throg
caseNote: Subject was a man transformed into a frog who became the Frog of Thunder using a sliver of Mjolnir. Associated with the Pet Avengers. Threat assessments are not to be based on height.
notes: No standalone article or infobox; Wikipedia's Thor supporting-cast list cites Thor #364-365 for Puddlegulp, and collector sources put his first appearance in #364. Wikipedia identifies the frog in Loki season 1 (voiced by Chris Hemsworth) as Throg, though it reads as a Thor variant.

name: Thunderball
caseNote: Subject is a physicist who invented a miniature gamma bomb, then gained Asgardian strength through the Wrecker's crowbar. Swings an enchanted wrecking ball for the Wrecking Crew. Holds a PhD; prefers the ball.
notes: Wikipedia categorizes him as a mutate, but his strength comes from the Wrecker's Asgardian-enchanted crowbar (magic).

name: Thunderstrike
caseNote: Subject is an architect whom Odin merged with Thor to save his life; he later served as Thor himself. Afterward operated as Thunderstrike, wielding an enchanted mace. Resume lists two unrelated careers.
notes: Two characters share the name; this is the original, Eric Masterson, not his son Kevin. Powers come first from Odin's merger with Thor and then from an enchanted mace, so magic vs tech is arguable; his Avengers tenure (Avengers #343-374) was as Thor.

name: Thundra
caseNote: Subject is a warrior from an alternate future ruled by women. Fought the Thing in the ring and has worked for and against the Frightful Four. Agents are advised not to challenge her to a match.
notes: Alignment contested: antihero vs villain. Origin contested: mutate (genetic enhancement) vs trained.

name: Tiger Shark
caseNote: Subject is a super-strong aquatic villain made so by Atlantean-derived experimentation, longtime rival of Namor. Has served with the Masters of Evil. Do not swim near.

name: Tigra
caseNote: Subject was transformed into a tiger-like humanoid by the Cat People after being mortally wounded as the Cat. Has served with the Avengers and the West Coast Avengers. Laser pointers are prohibited in her presence.
notes: Origin contested: Wikipedia lists her as a human mutate, but the Cat People's transformation combined science and sorcery. A friend named Greer (Nichele Lambert) in Hawkeye (2021) is fan-linked to her but never identified as Greer Grant Nelson, so not counted as an MCU appearance.

name: Tinkerer
caseNote: Subject is Phineas Mason, an elderly inventor who builds and repairs weapons for Spider-Man's enemies. Prefers to work behind the scenes. Agents are advised to inspect any repaired equipment for additions.
notes: His infobox lists the Masters of Evil, but neither his biography nor the Masters of Evil article supports it, so no team is set. The article body dates ASM #2 to April 1963, but the infobox and cover date say May 1963.

name: Titania
caseNote: Subject is a wrestler whose strength was boosted by the Beyonder. Frequent partner of the Absorbing Man. Agents are advised not to cut in line.
notes: Ms. Marvel snippet is only a photo reference.

name: Titanium Man
caseNote: Subject is a Soviet operative who donned massive green armor to defeat Iron Man in the name of his nation. Has also served with the Titanic Three. Results to date have not favored Subject.
notes: Several characters have used the name; the record follows the original, Boris Bullski.

name: Toad
caseNote: Subject is a leaping mutant who has served as Magneto's lackey. Later fought alongside the Defenders. Agents are advised not to ask about the warts.
notes: Alignment villain, though some stories cast him as comic relief.

name: Tombstone
caseNote: Subject is an albino hitman turned crime boss who grew up in Harlem. Exposure to an experimental gas left him with superhuman strength and durability. Agents are advised his name is less a threat than a forecast.
notes: Wikipedia's lead and infobox name him Alonzo Thompson 'Lonnie' Lincoln, while its biography says he was born Lonnie Thompson Lincoln. The infobox lists the Maggia and the Hand, but the text never describes him as a member, so no team is set. His MCU role is a brief cameo (Marvin Jones III) in Brand New Day's opening montage.

name: Toro
caseNote: Subject is the teenage partner of the original Human Torch. Can ignite himself and fly. Agents are advised not to give him matches.
notes: MCU snippets were Benicio del Toro.

name: Trapster
caseNote: Subject is an inventor of adhesive and trap devices, formerly known as Paste-Pot Pete. Frightful Four member and recurring opponent of the Human Torch. Agents should avoid sticky situations.
notes: Debut is as Paste-Pot Pete in Strange Tales #104; Trapster identity from Fantastic Four #38 (1965-05).

name: Triton
caseNote: Subject is an aquatic Inhuman with fish-like features who can survive the deepest oceans. Member of the Royal Family. Prefers to be wet.

name: Typhoid Mary
caseNote: Subject has multiple personalities and telekinetic powers. Has worked as assassin for the Kingpin and the Hand. Agents are advised to ask which personality is on duty.
notes: Origin mutant per Wikipedia infobox; her power source has been retconned over time. Debut as Mutant Zero (2007) is later.

name: Tyr
caseNote: Subject is the Asgardian god of war and eldest son of Odin. Lost his left hand to the wolf Fenris during its binding. Gloves are requisitioned for Subject one at a time.
notes: Alignment is mixed: mostly loyal to Asgard, but he has allied with Loki against Odin and commanded Hela's forces. 'God of War' is left out of aliases because it belongs primarily to Ares.

name: U.S. Agent
mcuFirst: The Falcon and the Winter Soldier
caseNote: Subject is a former Army soldier who underwent strength augmentation and briefly replaced Captain America. Has since served with the West Coast Avengers and the Thunderbolts. Agents should not call Subject the other guy with the shield.
notes: His comics powers come from the Power Broker's augmentation (Wikipedia: 'mutagenic augmentation'), classed here as a super-soldier enhancement program; the MCU version takes a super-soldier serum.

name: Uatu the Watcher
caseNote: Subject is a member of an alien race sworn to observe without interfering. Monitors Earth from a base on the Moon. Has repeatedly broken that oath for the good of humanity.
notes: mcu contested: false (Watchers cameo in Guardians Vol. 2 is unnamed; Uatu in Daredevil: Born Again S2 is a silhouette-style easter egg; named Uatu appearances are voice-only animation) vs true (Daredevil: Born Again S2 cameo, 2026-03). Alignment also contested: hero vs neutral.

name: Ulik
caseNote: Subject is the strongest of the Rock Trolls and a recurring foe of Thor, fighting with uru knuckle-dusters called pounders. Once rewrote history to replace Thor as the thunder god Tanarus. The substitution was not well reviewed.
notes: Rock Trolls are treated as a Norse mythological race (deity).

name: Ultron
caseNote: Subject is a robot built by Hank Pym that soon turned on its creator and the Avengers. Has rebuilt itself in hundreds of numbered versions, many with adamantium bodies. Unplugging has been attempted.
notes: Debut uses the cameo in The Avengers #54, where he appears as the Crimson Cowl; first full appearance is #55 (August 1968). He led the Masters of Evil in that debut story, a short stint left out of teams.

name: Valeria Richards
caseNote: Subject is the daughter of Reed and Sue Richards and a child prodigy of the highest order. Co-founded the Future Foundation. Agents are advised not to challenge her to a science fair.
notes: Origin contested: mutate (in-utero cosmic-ray exposure, super-genius) vs trained (intellect only).

name: Valkyrie (Brunnhilde)
caseNote: Subject leads the Valkyrior, Odin's shield-maidens, and was a mainstay of the Defenders. Founding member of the Secret Avengers, often seen riding the winged horse Aragorn. A parking permit for the horse remains pending.
notes: Infobox lists Thor #133 (Oct 1966, an unnamed Valkyrie cameo) ahead of the Enchantress's Valkyrie guise in Avengers #83 (Dec 1970) and the Barbara Norriss version in Defenders #4, which the lead calls her first appearance. Tessa Thompson's MCU Valkyrie is described by Wikipedia as a different version of the character and is not named Brunnhilde on screen.

name: Venom
caseNote: Subject is an alien symbiote first worn by Spider-Man as a black costume, later bonded to journalist Eddie Brock, who blamed Spider-Man for ruining his career. Has since operated as a violent 'Lethal Protector'. Subject refers to itself as 'we'; agents may do likewise.
notes: Debut uses the infobox's first entry, the symbiote as Spider-Man's alien costume (ASM #252, May 1984); Venom proper debuted with a cameo in ASM #299 (April 1988). The symbiote has had many hosts; realName follows Eddie Brock, and his temporary Sinister Six stint and Savage Avengers membership of unclear length are not counted.

name: Venus
caseNote: Subject is the Olympian goddess of love and beauty. Has appeared in comics since the 1940s. Agents are advised to avoid romantic complications.
notes: Venus #1 debut per infobox.

name: Veranke
caseNote: Subject is the Skrull Queen who replaced Jessica Drew and led the Secret Invasion. Impersonated Spider-Woman for years. Agents are advised to check ID.
notes: Infobox lists New Avengers #1 as Spider-Woman cover; first appearance as Veranke is New Avengers #40 (2008-06). Not in MCU cast.

name: Viper (Ophelia Sarkissian)
caseNote: Subject has served as a commander of Hydra and led the Serpent Squad. Immune to most toxins and venoms, and once forced Wolverine into marriage. Agents should not accept any drink Subject has poured.
notes: mcu is false: her live-action versions are in Fox's The Wolverine (2013) and ABC's Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D., neither of which counts. Wikipedia tags her 'human mutate', but her listed abilities are training plus toxin immunity; Hellfire Club and Hand ties were brief and are omitted.

name: Vision
caseNote: Subject is a synthezoid built by Ultron to destroy the Avengers, who joined them instead and later married the Scarlet Witch. Can alter his density at will, so locked doors should not be considered secure.
notes: Infobox lists the August 1968 publication date; the article gives the October 1968 cover date, used per rubric. Distinct from the 1940s Timely Vision (Aarkus).

name: Viv Vision
caseNote: Subject is a synthezoid built by the Vision from his and his wife's brainwaves as part of his attempt at a suburban family. She later joined the Champions. The experiment is not recommended for replication.
notes: Wikipedia covers her in a section of List of Marvel Comics characters: V, not in her own article. She is not in VisionQuest's cast list as of November 2026.

name: Volstagg
caseNote: Subject is the largest member of the Warriors Three and styles himself the Lion of Asgard. Heads a household full of children and once took up a hammer as the War Thor. Catering for joint operations should be tripled.
notes: Volstagg has no standalone Wikipedia article (it redirects to Warriors Three); debut and details come from that article.

name: Vulture
caseNote: Subject is Adrian Toomes, an elderly electronics engineer who built an electromagnetic flight harness and turned to crime after his business partner embezzled their profits. A founding member of the Sinister Six. Considered a flight risk.
notes: Others have used the Vulture name; this entry is Adrian Toomes, the original.

name: War Machine
caseNote: Subject is a former U.S. Marine pilot and Tony Stark's closest friend. Has worn the Iron Man armor in Stark's absence and later his own heavily armed War Machine suit. Subtlety was not a design requirement.

name: Warlock (Technarch)
caseNote: Subject is a shapeshifting Technarch alien that can turn into machines and weapons. Escaped his father and joined the New Mutants. Agents are advised to speak slowly and literally.
notes: Infobox flagged unreliable but the page is the right character. Origin alien (Technarch) vs synthetic; gender other (no gender, male-presenting).

name: Warpath
caseNote: Subject is an Apache mutant with superhuman strength, speed and senses, and the brother of the late John Proudstar. Has been a steady member of X-Force. Agents are advised to take a seat rather than argue.

name: Wasp (Janet van Dyne)
caseNote: Subject is a founding Avenger credited with naming the team. Shrinks to insect size, flies on wings and fires bio-electric stings. Agents should not mistake her for a pest.
notes: Origin contested: Wikipedia lists her as a human mutate (implanted Pym particles, wings from Pym's genetic modifications), while the MCU version uses a suit. MCU debut is Hayley Lovitt's nonspeaking flashback cameo in Ant-Man (2015).

name: Wendigo
caseNote: Subject is a cursed monster associated with cannibal spirits of northern folklore. Fought the Hulk and Wolverine. Agents are advised not to hike in the Canadian wilds.
notes: Several men have been the Wendigo; Paul Cartier is the original.

name: Werewolf by Night
caseNote: Subject carries a hereditary curse that makes him a werewolf under the full moon. Has served on monster-hunting teams. Agents are advised to check the lunar calendar.
notes: Origin: hereditary curse (magic) with Russoff bloodline.

name: Whiplash
caseNote: Subject is a mercenary armed with cybernetically controlled titanium whips. Has worked for the Maggia and repeatedly tangled with Iron Man. Agents should maintain a distance of at least one whip length.
notes: Mantle record anchored on the original, Mark Scarlotti; the MCU's Whiplash is Ivan Vanko (Mickey Rourke), an original character who inspired the comics' Anton Vanko Whiplash.

name: Whirlwind
caseNote: Subject is a mutant who spins at high speed to generate winds and cyclonic force. Has fought Giant-Man, the Avengers and Spider-Man. Agents are advised to keep a handhold available.
notes: Origin: infobox says human mutant (mutation and later alteration). Primary team contested.

name: White Rabbit
caseNote: Subject is Dr. Lorina Dodson, an heiress who spent her inheritance on Alice in Wonderland-themed gadgets for a life of crime. Fights with an umbrella that fires explosive carrots. Agents are advised not to follow her down any holes.

name: White Tiger (Hector Ayala)
caseNote: Subject is a martial artist who gained tiger-like abilities from mystic amulets. A founding member of the Sons of the Tiger. Agents are advised to leave the amulets alone.
notes: Infobox page is a shared article for several White Tigers; Hector Ayala's debut was used. Origin magic (amulets) vs mutate is arguable.

name: Wiccan
debutIssue: The Vision and the Scarlet Witch vol. 2 #12
caseNote: Subject wields reality-altering magic and is a founding member of the Young Avengers. Records identify him as the reincarnated son of the Scarlet Witch. His spells work best when he states exactly what he wants; this office asks the same of all applicants.
notes: Wikipedia's infobox lists the infant William Maximoff's first appearance (Vision and the Scarlet Witch #12, Sept 1986), while Billy Kaplan himself debuted in Young Avengers #1 (Apr 2005). Origin is set to magic because his powers are explicitly magical, though Wikipedia labels him a human mutant. A short 2021 Guardians of the Galaxy stint is left out.

name: Winter Soldier
caseNote: Subject was Captain America's wartime partner, presumed killed in 1945. Recovered by the Soviets, fitted with a cybernetic arm and used as a brainwashed assassin for decades. Has since served as Captain America himself.
notes: Infobox debut is as Bucky (1941); the Winter Soldier identity debuted in Captain America #6 (2005). Classed antihero (Wikipedia: 'a dark hero in search of redemption') and super-soldier via the Infinity Formula.

name: Wizard
caseNote: Subject is an inventor whose anti-gravity discs let him fly and hurl objects. Founded the Frightful Four to oppose the Fantastic Four. Agents will find the discs more fashionable than effective.
notes: Real name Bentley Wittman is widely given in the comics; mcu matches were unrelated uses of the word.

name: Wolfsbane
debutIssue: Marvel Graphic Novel #4: The New Mutants
caseNote: Subject is a Scottish-born mutant who shifts between human, wolf and hybrid forms. Raised by a strict minister, she has served on five rosters. Agents are advised not to call her a dog.
notes: Infobox cites 'The New Mutants (September 1982)', i.e. the graphic novel.

name: Wolverine
caseNote: Subject heals from nearly any injury and carries an adamantium-laced skeleton with three retractable claws per hand. Has served with the X-Men, the Avengers and X-Force, sometimes concurrently. Agents are advised not to ask his age.
notes: Infobox lists The Incredible Hulk #180 (Oct 1974); his first full appearance is #181 (Nov 1974). weapon-x is included for his iconic origin as that program's subject, and antihero follows the rubric's lethal-methods definition.

name: Wonder Man
caseNote: Subject is a Hollywood actor powered by ionic energy from Baron Zemo's treatments. Created to infiltrate the Avengers, he turned on Zemo and later joined the team. Autograph requests should go through proper channels.

name: Wong
caseNote: Subject is the longtime manservant and confidant of Doctor Strange. Trained in the mystic arts of Kamar-Taj and has served on several Avengers rosters. Agents are advised that he handles the household accounts.
notes: Comics Wong is a martial artist and mystic servant; magic chosen because the MCU and recent comics make him a sorcerer (trained is defensible).

name: Wrecker
caseNote: Subject is a fired demolition worker whose crowbar was enchanted by the Norn Queen Karnilla, who mistook him for Loki. Leads the Wrecking Crew. Subject is not to be issued tools.
notes: Powers come from Karnilla's enchantment of his crowbar (magic); one-off Frightful Four and Lethal Legion stints are left out.

name: Wyatt Wingfoot
caseNote: Subject is a Keewazi Native American athlete and friend of the Human Torch. Has served as a trusted ally to the Fantastic Four. Declined to wear a mask.

name: X-23
caseNote: Subject shares Wolverine's healing factor and has adamantium-coated claws, two in each hand and one in each foot. Raised as an assassin by the Facility before joining the X-Men and X-Force. Agents are advised to check her shoes.
notes: She debuted in the X-Men: Evolution episode 'X23' (aired 2003-08-02) before NYX #3 (Feb 2004). Wikipedia calls her a superheroine, though her assassin and X-Force past could support antihero; 'Wolverine' and 'Weapon X' are omitted as aliases because they belong to Logan.

name: Yelena Belova
caseNote: Subject is a Red Room-trained operative who spent years trying to supplant Natasha Romanova as the Black Widow. Has since served with S.H.I.E.L.D. and the Thunderbolts. Agents should not confuse the two.
notes: Wikipedia's infobox dates Inhumans #5 to January 1999, its on-sale month; the cover date is March 1999. A design sketch appeared earlier in Marvel Knights: Wave 2 Sketchbook #1 (January 1998).

name: Yon-Rogg
caseNote: Subject is a Kree military commander, Captain Mar-Vell's rival for Una. Has repeatedly tried to eliminate Mar-Vell. Agents are advised to avoid his command.

name: Yondu
caseNote: Subject is a blue Centaurian archer who commands his arrow by whistle. Founding member of the 31st-century Guardians. Agents are advised against whistling near him.
notes: Comics Yondu is a hero; MCU version is an antihero.

name: Zarathos
caseNote: Subject is a demon bound to the first Ghost Rider. Was imprisoned by Mephisto before returning. Agents are advised not to speak about it before dinner.

name: Zeus
caseNote: Subject is the ruler of the Olympian gods and wields thunderbolts. Father of Ares and Hercules; relations with both vary. Briefings involving Subject's family should allow extra time.
notes: Infobox debut is as Jupiter in Venus #5 (Jun 1949); he first appears as Zeus in Journey into Mystery Annual #1 (1965). Alignment is a judgment call: a morally gray ruler who alternates between ally and antagonist, including a comic antagonist in Thor: Love and Thunder.
